newsitem.title: MEXICO: FEATURE - When Mexican volcano blows, locals turn to shaman.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - When Mexican volcano blows, locals turn to shaman.

text.p: Every time Mexico's Popocatepetl volcano blows, residents of this farming town running precariously up its foothills ask what could be a life or death question: Should they leave?

Close enough that the rumbles in its belly shake the creaky wooden doors and tin roofs, that donkeys bray at the sight of hot rocks pounding down the mountainside, Xatlitzintla is in the firing line of a force of nature that threatens to bury them under a river of molten lava.

But when the volcano exploded last week and sent a canopy of ash hundreds of miles over southern Mexico, residents stayed put, pinning their faith on a local shaman who has the dubious honour of communicating with the volcano in his dreams.

"Popo's just grumbling. It's still not the moment," Antonio Analco told local town officials on Sunday night when shaken townspeople stood in the main square wondering whether to evacuate. "Nothing's going to happen."

The power of "Tiemperos" -- shamanistic diviners -- in the impoverished towns at the feet of Popocatepetl poses an unusual conundrum to officials who for three years have watched one of the world's major volcanos spring back to life.

The government has issued evacuation plans, set up hostels, started army patrols and shut off the 17,887-foot (5,465-metre) mountain in a bid to minimise loss of life if it ever blows its top. Even planes stear clear of the crater.
"We would have 10 or 12 minutes, no more," deputy mayor Antonio Perez Agustin told Reuters.
WHEN A SHAMAN SPEAKS, VILLAGERS LISTEN
But when it comes to the volcano, it is Analco, not the vulcanologists or emergency officials in brand-new jeeps, that capture this town's attention.
Analco is considered Popo's curator. Or, as is his family put it, manservant to a cranky old man who appears in his dreams and asks for favours to remain in good humour.

Recently, "Goyito" as the volcano is more fondly known, had a craving for music. Analco, who is so poor he sometimes sells peanuts on the street in Mexico City, was forced to find an accordian, a mandolin and a guitar to please him.
"I remember him when I was 16 and he used to flex his muscles, but now he's like me, old and cranky," Analco's mother-in-law Anselma said as she gazed up at Popo.

When a false rumour ran round the town in 1994 that former President Carlos Salinas had sold the volcano to Japan to pay off Mexico's massive debts, Analco, without dismissing the story, told residents Popo would get his own back.
The result: The Kobe earthquake in Japan in January 1995, according to Analco's wife Ines. "How on earth could Salinas sell the condemned old man. He's God's, not his," she said.

Now, Analco says, the volcano is issuing a warning that may be tied to the approaching end of the millennium -- a moment of potential cataclysm in the Nahuatl Indian culture and in the mystical Catholicism that pervades the town.
"All that is sown will be reaped at the end of the millennium," Ines said. "God will tell Goyito to rise up."
When and if it does "rise up", what will the locals do?
According to Perez Agustin, the deputy mayor, even the best-laid government plans to evacuate the town could come unstuck because residents may simply refuse to budge.

He said during the first big explosion in December 1994, the town had a terrible experience of evacuation. Residents fell ill, they were cooped up in tiny hostels, and their animals went unfed and died or fled.
NO PLAN TO SAVE THE ANIMALS
Even now there is no contingency plan for animals, he noted, in a town where life savings are not in the bank, but invested in turkeys and pigs that freely amble about.

Last week, army patrols in giant Humvee jeeps rumbled through the town, their guns at the ready. They are expected to safeguard the town from thieves if it is evacuated, but locals said they looked more threatening than benign.

According to Julio Glockner, an anthropologist who studies the diviners, the residents' Nahuatl roots make them susceptible to a fatalism that could mean they would rather perish than run if Popo sounds the death knell.
"It is a dialogue of the deaf," he said. "Both sides simply do not understand each other."
